query: For as-deposited, non-equiatomic FeMnNiGeSi-type high-entropy alloys intended for magnetic refrigeration, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs their magnetocaloric response and hysteresis during low-applied-field magnetic-cooling cycles? Earlier work focused mainly on arc-melted ingots and melt-spun microribbons, where an ordered single-phase hexagonal state undergoes a first-order magnetostructural transition that produces a large but sharp and hysteretic entropy change; these bulk forms also have limited heat-exchange rates because of their low surface-to-volume ratio. Prior searches have largely emphasized composition-dependent changes in transition temperature or response amplitude, with most studies pursuing only one optimization variable. Under the constraints of avoiding rare-earth elements, retaining mechanical stability and low cost, enabling rapid heat exchange, and limiting hysteretic losses, specify one controlled intervention that would distinguish the proposed governing explanation from alternatives, the predicted observations relative to the as-deposited baseline, the boundaries over which those predictions should hold, the prior observations that support the hypothesis, and a result that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: In as‐deposited, non‐equiatomic FeMnNiGeSi high‐entropy alloys, localized chemical inhomogeneities produce a broad distribution of exchange energies that govern the sharp, hysteretic first‐order magnetostructural transition. A controlled post‐deposition homogenization anneal that reduces these micro‐segregation effects will decrease hysteresis in the magnetocaloric response during low-applied-field cycles while maintaining a significant entropy change.
generation.material_initial_state: As-deposited FeMnNiGeSi alloys with a predominantly single-phase hexagonal structure that nevertheless exhibit nanoscale chemical inhomogeneity (micro-segregation) leading to a broad distribution of local exchange interactions.
generation.intervention: Apply a moderate-temperature, short-duration homogenization annealing treatment designed to promote chemical diffusion and reduction of micro-segregation without inducing substantial grain growth.
generation.conditions: Measurements performed under low-applied-field magnetic cooling cycles across the transition temperature range, comparing annealed samples to the as-deposited baseline. The alloys must meet constraints on avoiding rare-earth elements, maintain mechanical stability and low cost, and support rapid heat exchange.
generation.structural_mediator: Reduction in nanoscale chemical heterogeneity (i.e. a narrower distribution of exchange energies) due to annealing-induced homogenization.
generation.mechanism: The annealing treatment minimizes local variations in magnetic exchange interactions by dissolving segregated compositional clusters, thereby smoothing the magnetostructural transition. This uniformity reduces the energy barriers for transformation across the microstructure, decreasing hysteresis while still allowing a detectable magnetocaloric entropy change.
generation.predicted_outcome: Post-annealed samples will exhibit a less abrupt and less hysteretic magnetocaloric response than the as-deposited baseline, with the transition occurring over a slightly broader temperature range but with reduced energy loss during cycling.
generation.baseline: The as-deposited alloys show a large, sharp, and hysteretic entropy change due to the broad distribution of local exchange energies from chemical inhomogeneities.
generation.boundary: These predictions are expected to hold for non-equiatomic FeMnNiGeSi high-entropy alloys processed under similar conditions (i.e., absence of rare-earth elements, constraints on cost and mechanical stability), and when the annealing parameters are carefully controlled to prevent excessive grain growth or the emergence of secondary phases.
generation.uncertainty: The exact quantitative changes in hysteresis and magnetocaloric entropy change are uncertain and may vary with specific annealing temperatures and durations. Furthermore, the degree of initial chemical inhomogeneity may differ between batches, affecting the outcome.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of as-deposited non-equiatomic FeMnNiGeSi samples. Subject one set to the prescribed homogenization anneal and keep the other as a control. Perform consistent, low-applied-field magnetocaloric cycling while characterizing both magnetic behavior (magnetization and entropy change vs. temperature) and microstructure (using TEM/EDX to assess chemical homogeneity).
measurements: Magnetic hysteresis loop areas from magnetization vs. field curves
Microstructural analyses (e.g., TEM, EDX mapping) to quantify compositional homogeneity
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If annealed samples do not show a statistically significant reduction in hysteresis (i.e., similar loop areas) or if microstructural analysis fails to reveal improved chemical uniformity compared to the as-deposited baseline—while the overall magnetocaloric response remains equivalent—the hypothesis would be falsified.

cited_evidence.text:
Tunable magnetocaloric effect in transition metal alloys

Abstract: The unpredictability of geopolitical tensions and resulting supply chain and pricing instabilities make it imperative to explore rare earth free magnetic materials. As such, we have investigated fully transition metal based “high entropy alloys” in the context of the magnetocaloric effect. We find the NiFeCoCrPdx family exhibits a second order magnetic phase transition whose critical temperature is tunable from 100 K to well above room temperature. The system notably displays changes in the functionality of the magnetic entropy change depending on x, which leads to nearly 40% enhancement of the refrigerant capacity. A detailed statistical analysis of the universal scaling behavior provides direct evidence that heat treatment and Pd additions reduce the distribution of exchange energies in the system, leading to a more magnetically homogeneous alloy. The general implications of this work are that the parent NiFeCoCr compound can be tuned dramatically with FCC metal additives.
